chunks: CSA versus a regular op-amp. The question: What is the difference between a CSA and a regular opamp?
A current sense amplifier is really an op-amp (a general-purpose amplifier chip) wired as a difference amplifier, with the properties this job needs built in.
Its gain-setting resistors sit on the same chip and are trimmed to match. Its inputs can sit far above its own supply voltage, so it works on a high-side bus.
And its offset is often microvolts, not millivolts. A plain op-amp with loose resistors is more flexible and fine when the bus is low and accuracy is modest.
Think of a pair of shoes. Two shoes made together as a matched pair fit each other well.
Two shoes bought separately in the same size can still differ a little, and the mismatch makes you limp.
In a difference amplifier, the four resistors are the shoes: if they are not matched, the bus voltage leaks into the reading. On-chip resistors are the matched pair.
Input range is a separate limit: a regular op-amp's inputs must stay inside its own supply.
Higher gain makes the same resistor tolerance look better (CMRR ∝ 1+G) but even G = 200 needs about 0. 05 percent matching to reach 100 decibels. Discrete 0.
1 percent resistors land at 82 decibels for G = 50; an on-die trimmed network gets to 100 decibels or more.
Difference amplifier: an op-amp with four resistors that subtracts two inputs. Matched resistors: resistors whose ratios agree very closely, which gives high CMRR.
CMRR: how well the amplifier ignores voltage common to both inputs, in dB. Input common-mode range: the voltage range the inputs tolerate, usually limited by the supply.
Zero-drift amplifier: a design that cancels offset continuously, to a few microvolts.
Build a difference amplifier with gain 50 and 0. 1% resistors. Its worst-case CMRR is about (1 plus 50) over (4 times 0. 001) equals 12 750 , which is 82 decibels.
On a 48 volts bus the leakage is 48 over 12750 equals 3. 8 millivolts, which is 7. 5% of a 50 millivolts signal.
A CSA with 120 decibels CMRR leaks only 48 over 10 to the 6 equals 48 µV, 0. 1% of the signal.
The offset gap is similar: 1 millivolts on a 10 milliohms shunt is a 100 milliamps error, while 100 µV gives 10 milliamps. That is the whole idea.
"A CSA is a difference amplifier in an IC, but built for shunt sensing: its gain-setting resistors are on-die and trimmed so CMRR is 100 to 120 decibels, where discrete 0.
1 percent resistors give only about 80 decibels; its inputs can sit above its own supply so it works on a high-side bus; and its offset is microvolts rather than millivolts.
A plain op-amp is more flexible and fine when the bus is within the supply and accuracy is modest."
